finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. Replacing the switch at the brake pedal is a small job on the vehicles examined: every maker-stated time found for one switch is 0.2 to 0.3 hour. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2010 Elantra about $48-$208 (0.3-1.2 hr); midsize 2011 Sonata about $61-$227 (0.3-1.2 hr); truck 2006 Colorado about $58-$255 (0.2-1.2 hr); luxury 2008 Acura MDX about $102-$301 (0.2-1.2 hr). The three benchmarks sit inside those totals: $80-$100, $82-$120 and a $183 average for one model. The low ends pair an online parts price with a warranty time, which is less than a shop charges for either, and many shops bill a minimum labor charge, so a supportable site range for the switch alone is roughly $75-$250, with the Acura-type switch that lists at $109 toward the top. How solid the labor times are: all four low ends are maker warranty times for the example vehicle and for one switch (Hyundai 0.3 M/H for the 2007-2010 Elantra and the 2011 Sonata, GM 0.2 labor hours for the 2004-2006 Colorado, Acura 0.2 hour for the 2007-11 MDX); the GM procedure also has the technician look at the switch retainer. All four high ends rest on one weak source: a general repair guide with no named author that says 0.8 to 1.2 hours at a shop or dealer, which is not a book time and not vehicle-specific. Subaru's 0.5 hour for its brake lamp switch recall is a cross-check only, because that kit also includes an adapter harness and a clevis pin. Because four of the eight labor range ends are not for the example vehicle, confidence is low. Parts: the high in every class is the maker's list price from a dealer parts catalog. No aftermarket switch was found on a page that states the part is new, so each low is a dealer-parts discounter's price for the genuine switch on a page that states it is new; aftermarket switches seen without a stated condition were $14.76-$15.49 for the Hyundais and $15.46 for the Colorado. Switch prices vary a lot within one model: the 2010 Elantra page also lists a $50.11 switch, and other Acura MDX years use switches that list from $12.40 to $125.46. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or electrical testing fee, shop supplies and sales tax, and many shops bill a minimum labor charge. Bulbs, a blown fuse, a damaged connector or wiring repair are quoted separately. Some vehicles need the switch adjusted or a sensor relearned with a scan tool, and a few need a software update afterward. On some vehicles the pedal stopper pad that presses the switch is replaced at the same time.
held_reason: Held at review after one attempt: all four labor highs rest on one unsigned general guide (2CarPros, 0.8 to 1.2 hours). Lows are maker times (Hyundai 0.3 M/H, GM 0.2, Acura 0.2 hour; the Hyundai figure re-read and matched). One signed or trade-press upper time would pass it.
